notes.meaning: King Jabin of Hazor heard about Israel's victories in the south and summoned other northern kings to join him in battle. Hazor was the leading city in the region, and Jabin was likely a royal title passed down like Pharaoh. These rulers realized they had to unite immediately to stop Israel. When God's people move forward in faith, opposition often gathers against them.

Jabin sent messengers across northern Canaan, gathering kings from the mountains, the valleys south of the Sea of Galilee, and the western seacoast. Different groups such as the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, and Hivites all answered the call. Even though these nations had their own rivalries, they joined together to fight against God's people.

The allied kings assembled a massive army with so many foot soldiers they seemed like grains of sand on the seashore. They also brought a huge number of horses and iron war chariots, which were the most terrifying military weapons of that day. They set up camp together at the waters of Merom to launch a united strike against Israel.

The Lord told Joshua not to fear this giant army, promising that by the next day Israel would defeat them all. God commanded Joshua to cut the leg tendons of their horses and burn their chariots so Israel would not keep them for war. God wanted His people to trust in His protection rather than in military power.

Joshua marched his entire army quickly and attacked the allied camp by surprise at the waters of Merom. This sudden assault caught the kings unprepared and threw their forces into immediate disorder. Bold action guided by God's promise wins the day.

The Lord handed the enemy over to Israel, who struck them down and chased the fleeing soldiers toward Sidon on the coast and east into the valley of Mizpeh. Israel won this massive battle through hard fighting rather than visible miracles, showing that God works through ordinary means. The victory was complete, leaving no surviving fighters.

Joshua obeyed the Lord's instructions without hesitation. He crippled the captured war horses and set fire to all their chariots. He refused to hold on to valuable weapons that might tempt Israel to rely on human might instead of God.

After the pursuit, Joshua turned back to capture Hazor and put its king to death with the sword. Hazor had been the leading royal city of the northern kingdoms and had started the whole alliance against Israel. Because it was the center of the rebellion, it faced swift and direct judgment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Archaeologists have uncovered a massive, fortified city at Hazor that covered about 200 acres and was destroyed by a fierce fire in the 13th century B.C., matching its biblical role as the leader of the region.

notes.meaning: The Israelites killed everyone inside Hazor, carrying out God's judgment against a corrupt society. Joshua then burned the entire city to the ground. Hazor was one of only three cities in Canaan that Joshua destroyed completely by fire.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that while Hazor was burned during this era, the destruction could have been carried out by Egypt, the Sea Peoples, or a rival Canaanite power, though Joshua remains a possible cause.

notes.meaning: Joshua captured all the northern royal cities and executed their rulers. He devoted the people to destruction, fulfilling the exact command God had given through Moses. Joshua did not act out of personal cruelty, but as God's servant carrying out divine justice.

Israel did not burn down the other captured cities that stood on mounds or hills, sparing them from fire. Leaving these hill towns intact was practical, because their raised locations made them easy to defend and ready for Israel to occupy. Hazor was the only northern city Joshua burned, because it had led the uprising.

The Israelites kept the livestock and goods of these cities as plunder for their own families. At the same time, they killed all the inhabitants, leaving no survivors who might lead them into idol worship. God enriched His people with these goods to give them a solid start in the land.

The Lord gave His instructions to Moses, Moses passed them on to Joshua, and Joshua followed them completely. Joshua made sure that not a single command given by the Lord was neglected. Faithful leaders show their loyalty by doing all that God directs.

These verses review the broad territory Joshua conquered across Canaan, extending from the southern desert of the Negev all the way north to Mount Hermon. Joshua captured the kings of these diverse regions, including the mountains, foothills, and valleys, and put them to death. This sweeping campaign demonstrated that God was faithfully giving Israel the entire land He had promised.

Joshua fought against these kings over several years rather than finishing the conquest in one quick campaign. God chose to subdue the land gradually so it would not become empty and overgrown with wild beasts. This long struggle also trained Israel in patience and steady reliance on God.

No city made a peace treaty with the Israelites except the Hivite citizens of Gibeon, who had used a trick to save their lives. Every other city chose to fight and had to be taken by force. The Canaanites had seen God's great deeds, but they stubbornly refused to ask for peace.

The Lord hardened the hearts of the Canaanites so that they would come out to fight Israel and face complete destruction. Because they loved their wicked ways and turned away from God's light, God handed them over to their own stubborn pride. Their defeat was the direct result of divine judgment on long-standing sin.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian writers such as Origen explained this hardening spiritually, seeing the Canaanites as pictures of sinful desires that believers must completely destroy in their own hearts.

notes.meaning: Joshua wiped out the Anakim from the hill country around Hebron and throughout the mountains of Judah and Israel. These giant warriors had terrified Israel's spies forty years before, but they were now easily defeated by God's power. The only remaining Anakim survived in the Philistine coastal cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod.

Joshua secured the whole land according to everything the Lord had promised Moses, breaking all major enemy resistance. He then divided the land among the tribes of Israel as their permanent inheritance, and the land finally enjoyed rest from war. God always keeps His word to those who follow Him.
